Review for We Were Here Expeditions: The FriendShip (Free)
🕹️ Playtime: 1–2 hours
👍 Rating: Very Positive

"A clever, communication-driven co-op game that tests your friendship in the best (and funniest) way possible!"

We Were Here Expeditions: The FriendShip is a short and sweet co-op puzzle game that revolves entirely around communication and teamwork. You and your partner are placed in separate locations and must solve puzzles by describing what you see and listening carefully to each other. It's a fun and often hilarious experience, especially when you think you're being clear—but your friend hears something completely different.

The game offers just the right amount of challenge without being too stressful. It's ideal for friends or couples looking for a bonding activity—or for testing how well you actually work together. And since it’s free-to-play, it’s a fantastic introduction to the “We Were Here” series.

Pros:

Unique puzzles focused on voice-only communication

Great for building (or testing) friendships

Fun and funny moments guaranteed

Easy to learn, quick to complete

Free-to-play, no commitment needed

Cons:

Very short—only takes about an hour or two

Requires a friend to play (no solo option)

Limited replay value once you know the solutions

If you're looking for a quick co-op game that combines puzzle-solving with a lot of laughs (and maybe a little yelling), The FriendShip is a must-try. 🎙️🧩😂

I believe that I'm missing some context for this game. It was a fine standalone experience, well worth the €2.79 I've paid for it (for the other person), but it feels more like a paid demo than a game. The assets are very high-quality, it's fully voice-acted, and…there's an ad for We Were Here Forever at the end. It all just feels a bit strange.

[h1] General Overview and Criticism [/h1]
The game itself consists of an intro and three minigames. Completing each minigame will earn you a ticket – bronze, silver, or gold – based on your performance. I've played this game through twice with my girlfriend and I believe we are both decent at video games, but some of the game design feels a bit unfair. All three minigames grade you based on your attained score, but only one of them (Maps & Markers) is designed to be played all the way through before you are given a verdict – both other games can be failed midway through, and if you have met the minimum requirement for at least a bronze ticket, you are forced to take it and continue on, without being able to retry. The host also sounds very disappointed at you in these cases, which only rubs the salt in, even if you don't feel like the failure was fully your fault. In the absence of a chapter select, this makes it difficult to want to go back and try again from the very beginning.

Below are my opinions about the game's separate segments – [b]SPOILERS AHEAD[/b]!

[h1] Intro [/h1]
The intro is organic and a nice hidden tutorial. I like how the game lets you subtly choose who goes on which side (the player who ends up being on the left side holds the way open for the other person), so you can switch without changing who is hosting.

[h1] Crewmate Carousel [/h1]
Unfortunately, this minigame isn't a strong start. Your first challenge immediately ends up being a time-limited one. The game doesn't progress in difficulty, so you only have a few seconds to act each round all the way through. There is a role-switch partway through the game and you are given no time to readjust – if you fail at this ‘choke point,’ you have already passed the bronze level, and so you cannot try again.

[h1] Maps & Markers [/h1]
This one is easily my favourite – I would love to play it again outside of this video game. It is essentially an oversized board game where each player has their own board with different designs and mechanics, but they must work together to attain the highest possible score. I absolutely adored the art style in this part – it reminded me of old fantasy games I've played as a child, like Rayman. This is also the only game where the point tresholds feel well thought-out – unless you actually understand the game, it is impossible to score enough points for even a bronze ticket. Unfortunately, the game is pretty light in its explanation, and I only truly understood [i]how[/i] to effectively work together once I've experienced both sides for myself.

[h1] Siren's Curse [/h1]
Here, one player is being shown a false world, and the other person must guide them through the real one while helping them avoid obstacles. I think the idea and design for this one is great…or at least for the parts we actually got to experience. Here, too, the bronze ticket's treshold is way too low in my opinion. We've failed relatively early in both of our playthroughs, and were dragged away by the game without being able to try again. There was also a timer puzzle that seemed to change the timing without warning, so even if you trust your guide, the game might screw the both of you over, anyway…

Despite its shortcomings, I still thought this was a fun game. I also do believe the problems it currently has could be easily solved with a patch; just…
[list]
    [*]Raise the bronze ticket's points requirement for Crewmate Carousel and Siren's Curse, so people can try again if they fail at the beginning
    [*]Give a little more time for each round in Crewmate Carousel, and also more time to react to the role-change
    [*]Let players try again even if they've reached the points tresholds for each minigame and/or add a chapter select
[/list]

Also, pleeease make Maps & Markers a real board game. I would buy it immediately.

I played We Were Here: The Friendship with a friend, and while I enjoyed it, it’s by far the shortest entry in the series—much shorter than the others, which are already relatively brief experiences.

The graphics are not great, staying consistent with the visuals of previous games in the series, but the artistic direction remains strong. The atmosphere and design make up for the technical shortcomings, creating a charming and engaging world.

The game offers three trials, each focused heavily on cooperation. They’re fun and well-designed, requiring solid communication to solve. The challenges are engaging enough to encourage replayability, especially if you’re aiming to get 100%. My friend and I managed to achieve 12/12 trophies, so we fully completed the game, which added to the satisfaction.

While I liked the experience overall, it’s undeniably too short. The brevity left us wanting more, especially since the core cooperative gameplay is so enjoyable.

We Were Here: The Friendship is a fun and creative co-op game, but its length limits its impact. If you’re a fan of the series, it’s worth playing—but don’t expect it to last long.

[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]

After the bitter disappointment of ‘we were here forever’ (WWHFE), coming into We Were Here FriendShip (WWHFS) was a positive breath of fresh air and a reminder of why I love this series. This little episode see’s a return to form with shorter, punchier, and more team oriented puzzles. 

The We Were Here series is a cooperative adventure where you need to communicate to overcome puzzles and, historically, uncover the story. Do you have a friend that thinks they’re a great communicator? Are you that person? Do you want to prove them/yourself right/wrong? If yes, then this is the series for you! 

As always (for that added challenge) forgo your discord, your skype, your steam voice, and just use the walkie-talkies. And if you’re finding THAT too easy, try it with someone whose native language isn’t your own! 

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The puzzles having different success criteria was really nice. We chose to go for gold, and persevered until we had a boat befitting our friendship. It was a really nice touch. 
[*] The voice acting, animation, puzzles, and maps felt well thought out and were nicely done. It’s amazing how even though this game had more reused assets, technically more back and forth, and the same overly long cut scenes format, it doesn’t feel grating or trying. 
[*] While this little episode has only three puzzles, they were varied and challenging enough that it felt good to play through. 
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Lag played a very negative role at several points in this game. Eventually we could account for it… But watching your partner plummet through an object rendered on your screen, but not yet on theirs, feels bad. 
[*] Being so short, the game felt like it ended just as it was getting going. 
[*] Many of the maps are poorly lit at points, especially if you’re attempting to improve on the score of a puzzle. Making some navigation unwieldly. 
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
[list][*] A slightly different animation each time the boat gets its work done. 
[*] Somehow reduce the lag a little. While only a quarter of a second, it made a difference. 
[*] A little more polish. There were textures which clipped, and a few parts which weren’t well signposted, but nothing game breaking or which couldn’t be worked out quickly enough. 
[/list]


[b][u]Overall Recommendation:[/u][/b]
After WWHFE, I thought the series might be done. They were moving away from fun, and interesting, and subtle into pointlessly over long exposé. This little shot of joy was exactly what I needed to feel good about the series again.

We both came into this game sceptical. We both hugely enjoyed it. 

I often say I don’t recommend games with a greater cost in pounds than hours to play… This one actually meets that metric on sale, but the time went superfast. I don’t feel like I played for 3 hours, and was surprised. And frankly that’s a great recommendation right there. This entire game felt shorter than a single one of the cut scenes in WWHFE, and was more enjoyable by orders of magnitude.

I recommend this for people who are looking for a co-op team building game, a short but intense test to their relationship, or a way to test and improve their own communication skills. 

I do not recommend you play this with anyone you want to remain friends with… or if you don’t have anyone to play with. You really do need that bond to make it special. 

Overall this is well worth it on sale, and a rare gem I think could be worth it off sale. The real kicker is knowing its short and sweet. This isn’t a full priced game and you’re not getting one. You’re getting three fun puzzles that are challenging and will push you to communicate more effectively. 

So go grab a friend, and build your Friend Ship.

I give this game a 71% rating: it's nice, nothing great, but nothing really bad either. It is probably a higher rating than it should only because I have been playing the whole series of We Were Here with the same good friend of mine, and now it is a very cosy and pleasant journey we keep having. For someone who is expecting a lot from an Escape Room/Coop Puzzle type of game, you would probably rate this lower (around the 50% mark), but for someone who never played a single game like that, has a good friend online, a couple of hours tonight and a few dollars... this is a really nice little game!

Admittedly the game is a bit clunky, the difficulty balance is all over the place (very easy puzzle, then suddenly stressful, then suddenly VERY hard and abstract, then suddenly based on skill and platform abilities...) and the length is very, very short (one evening). Also, the music and narration tend to be annoying and tedious, and there is close to no story.
But beside that? the environments are lovely and quite crafted, the overall vibe is reminiscent to Disney Parks Pirates of the Caribbean or Sea of Thieves, some puzzle like the last one are very imaginative and original, and getting all the achievements should still be a bit of a challenge for you and your friend.
...and less than 5 bucks!

We Were Here Expeditions: The FriendShip, developed by Total Mayhem Games, is a bite-sized cooperative puzzle adventure that takes the core concepts of the We Were Here series—communication, teamwork, and asymmetrical problem-solving—and distills them into a more accessible, lighter experience. Designed as a free-to-play entry point into the franchise, it stands apart from its more narrative-heavy predecessors by emphasizing fun over mystery, camaraderie over tension, and rapid engagement over prolonged exploration. Despite its shorter runtime and lighter tone, The FriendShip remains a compelling exercise in coordination and trust between two players, reinforcing the series’ central tenet: nothing is more powerful than clear communication.

The premise is straightforward. Two players find themselves stranded in a strange amusement park-like environment filled with whimsical, carnival-themed puzzles that can only be solved through precise verbal communication. Unlike previous We Were Here titles, which leaned into atmospheric storytelling and high-stakes escapes, The FriendShip is more playful, though no less challenging. There's still a sense of urgency, but it’s wrapped in bright colors, carnival music, and game-show aesthetics. The lighter tone makes it an ideal introduction for those new to cooperative puzzle games or those looking to test the waters with a friend without committing to a longer title.

Gameplay centers on pairs of asymmetrical puzzles that require both players to convey what they see, hear, or do in order to progress. These challenges test a range of communication skills, from spatial description to sound identification, symbol matching, and timed coordination. The strength of the design lies in its minimalism—there’s no inventory system or complex mechanics to manage, just you and your partner, separated physically in-game but connected by voice. This core loop, familiar to series veterans, feels sharper and more refined here. The puzzles are cleverly constructed and reward clear, deliberate dialogue. Miscommunication can lead to hilarious failure, but the stakes are low enough that it encourages experimentation rather than punishing mistakes.

One of the most refreshing aspects of The FriendShip is how it gamifies teamwork itself. Players receive scores at the end of each puzzle based on their performance, and can earn bronze, silver, or gold medals depending on how efficiently and precisely they collaborate. These scores add a layer of replayability and competition, enticing duos to retry puzzles in pursuit of a perfect run. The feedback system encourages introspection—were we too vague? Did we mishear something? Could we have come up with a better way to describe that symbol? It turns each session into a kind of cooperative self-improvement challenge, without ever feeling too serious or demanding.

Visually, the game is a bright departure from the icy, foreboding aesthetics of earlier entries in the franchise. The carnival-themed environments are quirky and colorful, filled with oversized props, themed rides, and whimsical contraptions. Despite being clearly built on a limited budget, the art direction is charming and cohesive. It complements the lighter tone without sacrificing the series’ distinctive style. The sound design, likewise, is functional and thematically appropriate—there’s plenty of auditory feedback to support puzzle-solving, and the voice proximity and clarity are fine-tuned for effective player communication, which is absolutely essential in a game like this.

Though short—the game can be completed in around 30 to 60 minutes—it feels well-paced and complete in what it aims to deliver. It doesn't overstay its welcome, nor does it feel undercooked. Its brevity is a strength, allowing it to act as both a standalone experience and a gateway into the broader We Were Here universe. For returning fans, it offers a welcome twist on the formula; for newcomers, it’s an approachable, low-stakes introduction that captures the magic of the series’ core mechanic: talking your way out of a puzzle together. While some might wish for more depth or a longer campaign, the game’s tight design and focus make it feel intentional rather than incomplete.

We Were Here Expeditions: The FriendShip is a masterclass in cooperative design distilled to its purest form. It strips away the narrative heft and dark tone of its predecessors, offering a bright, replayable, and engaging puzzle experience that lives and dies on the strength of your partnership. In doing so, it underscores what makes the We Were Here series special: not the setting, not the puzzles, but the human connection between two players trying to understand each other under pressure. Whether you’re testing a new friendship or celebrating an old one, this expedition is well worth taking.

There are also hints for each level so you don't have to stress too much if you want to finish the game quickly. The levels were creative and challenging also very fun to play through.

We Were Here Expeditions: The Friendship is a two person co-op puzzle game where you must work with a friend to escape an abandoned amusement park. There are three different puzzle rooms that must be solved via communication with your partner. 

Overall, I found this title to be the best of the entire series, which is somewhat amusing given it was free for a weekend and of the titles listed for a price, it's the cheapest. It is relatively short (comparable to the first title in the series, which is/has been always free to play). Whereas other titles in this series feature much less clear puzzles, each puzzle in this game was more obvious. Now, you might think that takes away some of the fun, but I found it didn't. Instead, it allows you to focus on solving the puzzle as opposed to trying to figure out what the puzzle even is to begin with. 

One playthrough took ~2 hours and a second playthrough for achievements (getting the max score for each puzzle) took another ~2 hours (mostly due to some RNG in the second puzzle). If a co-op puzzle game sounds like something you'd enjoy, I'd recommend this game. That said, I definitely recommend playing the original as it is free and will give you a good sense of the type of gameplay you'll be getting into.

We Were Here Expeditions is the 5th entry in the We Were Here series, but is instead a more bite sized game. Unlike the other entries, this one does not have any story or mysteries to it, but hosts 3 distinct puzzles, without sacrificing any of the quality of the previous games.

The first is a reaction time puzzle, in which you have to quickly describe a picture to your partner before the time runs out. Sounds simple enough, but it remains challenging and varied enough.

The second is a co-operative puzzle where you have to find the piece which best works for both of you. You may have a great piece on your side, but it may be terrible for your partner, which is where the challenge lies in picking the right piece.

The last is a trust fall like exercise, where you have to guide your partner through a series of obstacles that they cannot see or react to.

Oh and I almost forgot to mention, but they released this one for free for the first few days, which was a really nice thing to do, but even at full price, it is more then worth it to buy it for a quality experience with a mate.

[h2] Introduction [/h2]
We Were Here Expeditions: The FriendShip is a cooperative escape room puzzle game developed by Total Mayhem Games. It's another entry in the We Were Here series. In this part, we focus on repairing the ship in order to escape from the abandoned amusement park. The developers offered the game for free for a limited time, so I was able to claim it at no cost.
[h2] Gameplay [/h2]
The core of the game lies in its cooperative gameplay. Players control separate characters, unable to see each other directly. Escape requires constant communication via walkie-talkie, describing their surroundings and collaborating on solutions. This mechanic is consistent with previous games in the WWH series.
[h2] Graphics [/h2]
While it may not be groundbreaking graphically, there's nothing to complain about. The graphics are pleasing to the eye, effectively capturing the atmosphere of the setting, and the level design is very well executed.
[h2] Sound Design [/h2]
Since communication relies heavily on walkie-talkie use, clear and well-crafted audio is essential. The game delivers, with crisp voice transmission, good environmental sounds and pleasant music.
[h2] Story [/h2]
We have exposition and justification for our actions, but the story has never been the main focus of these games, and the same is true here. However, that's okay for the game.
[h2] Enjoyment and Replayability [/h2]
Solving puzzles with a friend brings a huge level of satisfaction and is extremely fun. While the core story can be completed in a single sitting, the game offers some replayability. We can replay challenges to achieve better results. While a bronze ticket is enough to pass, in good company, attempts to obtain a gold ticket are never dull.

If this is your first We Were Here game, don't. Start with the main series. This standalone has puzzles that require timing, jumping and platforming skills, which is largely absent from the others. Very mixed on this one. I don't mind the shorter runtime too much. The puzzles are usually fun, have a lot of nice moments when you finally figure out the puzzle. I think the part where the shorter runtime hurts is that if you do not like/understand one of the puzzles, that's about 1/3 of the game. The idea is they're replayable to get a better score, though the process to do so can be a bit annoying. Me and my brother personally only tried most like, two times (one when we still were learning rules, one more to actually pass). The one we tried the most was the final one, but this one actually was one of the ones with an issue for us. There are moving platforms you have to guide the other player through, but you would end up falling through rather than landing on the platform. This was frustrating because it was 1, the fifth obstacle, and 2 felt completely out of our hands. We solved the actual puzzle portion but due to how the game was we still failed. It being the last part we did might've soured my opinion on it more than if it was earlier honestly. But it can be fun to play with someone (especially if neither of you are particularly interested in getting the best score), but the level of quality from the other games really make this one feel weak in comparison. Maybe the issue we faced was only for us though, feel free to try it and form your own opinions on it.

Like its predecessors, We Were Here Expeditions is a first-person puzzler with online coop for two players.  The puzzles in this one have much more of a "mini-game" feel than the previous ones.  Each of the three puzzles can be beaten with a "bronze", "silver", or "gold" rating.

The first puzzle, like many of their previous puzzles, involves communicating symbols over the mic.  Unlike puzzles in their previous games, this one has a time limit.  There's three increasingly-difficult sections with separate time-limits.  You're almost guaranteed to fail your first attempt, meaning you'll have to do the entire thing over multiple times if you want the gold.  Unfortunately when we beat the gold challenge, the "success" and "failure" sounds played at the same time and we were only awarded silver.  We did it again, and the same thing happened again. It seems to just be completely broken.

The second puzzle is a board game.  While it is unique and I enjoyed it, it has a heavy randomness element, which is a terrible idea for a puzzle game. Even if your strategy is perfect, you might still be denied a gold due to bad RNG, which is what happened to us.

The third puzzle is one of those mazes where nasty surprises await.  When you fail, you need to start from the beginning.  What this ultimately means is doing the maze over and over and [i]over[/i] until you've mastered all the tricks.  One of the tricks was completely broken and led to us continuously falling through the floor (yes, the real floor) when we shouldn't have.

In this game, the developers experimented with new ideas, which is great.  Unfortunately, none of them work.  Even if they weren't buggy messes, the core ideas are just not fun. This is by far the worst game of the series that I've played.

[h1] This Review Contains Minor Plot Spoilers (It's worth the read if you value sanity)[/h1]

We Were Here Expeditions: The FriendShip, is probably the most challenging we were here game I've played, not because it requires using your noggin to the point of it turning to a puddle, not because of the random element nature of the game, but, because I cant go 5 seconds without me and my partner having some kind of connection issue. This is the only We Were Here game we have played with this issue.

We Were Here Expeditions: The FriendShip, is a game that sounds great on paper, but in practice leads to what feels and looks like a game of chance. I don't think anyone who has played The Friendship is under the Illusion that this isn't a game of chance, why do I say this?

Well From the opening couple minutes (and the trailer), you see you are in a carnival, once you and your partner split into your sides, you are presented with an introduction to the ticket system, there are three kinds of ticket, a reset, bronze, silver and gold ticket, reset being you have to play the game again and gold being the best ticket, these tickets upgrade your boat in various ways (however I cant say fully to what extent as we played till we got gold tickets and didn't settle for anything less). 

I wont go into too much specifics beyond that as to avoid heavy spoilers, their are 3 puzzles total.

The first gave us the most trouble as with our lag we had issues where the timer would start and run out before my partner could even see the curtains fully open (this was due to lag issues). 

Puzzle 2, we didn't have to compete with time but random elements, sure their is some element of skill to this game, we had several rounds where we got close however wound up being impossible to complete because the necessary tiles or towers we needed did not spawn in on the final round meaning we have to restart the entirety of puzzle 2 for the gold ticket. After a few more hours, a mental breakdown and the rng gods blessing us we completed puzzle 2, It defiantly is a step up in challenge from the 1st puzzle however, it mostly comes down to an unhealthy amount of luck and a fair bit of thinking, I would say the side placing towers is easier that the side placing colour patterns (Wont say more than that as to not delve to heavily into spoilers.) 

Today we completed Puzzle 3, I will say puzzle 3 is probably the favourite of them all, however, if your like us and you have severe and frequent lag issues, then you will have problems with this puzzle. However, we found that a lot of this puzzle can be memorised and with a bit of counting and listening can complete a large majority without your partners help, their was only 2 sections in the final puzzle that required the aid of my partner.

Talking a bit further on network connectivity, I will stress this again this is the most buggy We Were here game we have played, boats starting off with one person in then, clipping through things, puzzles bugging out, issues before we have even got into proper gameplay, this is BY FAR the buggiest We Were Here Game.

All that aside however, the game is that We Were Here art style we all know and love, with the music to boot, I also am also a fan of the carnival look and feels they have manged to achieve, the corny lines from a pre-recorded voice, the tunnel of love feel (although technically its probably closer to something like Disneyland "It's a small world after all" or "Pirates of the Caribbean" feel with animatronics), theirs also posters for you to ogle at and a map of the park at the entrance, this place is dripping with that theme park charm.

To close this out however I will have to give this game a not recommended, even on sale, as this game was as previously stated the most buggy and with the lag experienced through our entire playthrough this caused the puzzles to be a slog to get through, on top of fighting the random chance nature of these games, I do applaud that this is thematically correct and an interesting idea and their where certainly some parts that where enjoyable, sadly their were enough issues and being a person thats not overly keen on random chance games, I could not fully enjoy it.

The last puzzle has a real big problem with latency as despite hosting a party i still had a 300 ping making the octopus zone completely annoying to get through as i had to jump from a VERY specific spot while walking in order to delay my landing long enough to actually land on the platforms and not fall through them making the entire last "puzzle" a horrible experience, if you play this game and see on the menu that you have higher than 150 ping i just would not recommend playing this game. - the 3rd one is the worst of all. This is mostly a platforming trial with many mini challenges where communication is key. The tutorial for the main concept of that trial is innexistant, so you might first not understand what you need to do as the observer, and on the top of that, you will not understand why the observer is key in that trial. Actually, you might not even understand that you are an actual observer. The timings are too tight to feel fair for both players on the second mini challenge. And while this trial is about communication, you will restart it so often that the non-observer player will end up learning by heart what to do, and the communication is reduced to strict minimum. Oh, and the best is that if you have a disconnection, you are frozen... Did I mention the tight timmings?

I would really not recommend this episode, and after playing two of them I believe I wouldn't continue the "We were here" series.

For the record, I have played both games with a person I have excellent communication, with whom I have solved countless IRL and virtual escapes rooms.
